title: Hosted API Chat Labs - parameter playbook & resiliency
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted chat/text generation. Covered streaming behavior, key parameters (temperature, top_p, tokens), retry/backoff strategies, and quick console tour for monitoring. Discussed security needs (SOC2, KMS) and next steps for a short POC and benchmark run against BrightWave's triage assistant workload.

Diego to provision sandbox project and API keys for BrightWave and run initial triage benchmark (by 2027-05-18)
Laura to share security questionnaire; Redwood to return SOC2/HIPAA notes and KMS integration guide (by 2027-05-17)
Schedule 30-min POC kickoff with engineering (target week of 2027-05-24)

transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-05-11 15:00 UTC | Duration 42m
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (BrightWave CTO), Evan Park (Platform Eng), Laura Gibbs (Security), Tom Reynolds (Product)

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we're excited to walk through a quick hosted chat labs session, just a practical demo — not too theoretical — of how you'd set up streaming, tune params, and handle retries with Redwood. Maya — thanks for taking the time.
[00:15] Maya: Yeah thanks. We're trying to figure out whether to go hosted or reserved. Main things are latency (sub-300ms ideally on short prompts), cost per triage request, and security.
[00:29] Avery: Totally, and we'll hit those. Diego will do a quick live sandbox run and I'll call out the config tradeoffs.
[00:38] Diego: Alright I'm sharing my screen — can everyone see the console? (screen share noise)
[00:46] Evan: Yep we can see it.
[00:48] Diego: Cool. So this is the hosted project, we created a sandbox API key scoped to generation:chat, and I'm using the conversation API. First thing to note is streaming — we stream deltas as they generate, you get low-latency partial tokens, which matters for your triage UI where we show incremental suggestions.
[01:05] Tom: Quick q — do we get token-level timestamps or just chunked events?
[01:09] Diego: It's chunked events, each event includes token fragments and an index. You can stitch locally if you need per-token timing; we also surface latency per event in the console metrics. Note: sometimes transcripts show 'kayv cache' in logs because of auto-captioning but it's actually KV cache.
[01:28] Avery: We'll also show fallback behavior if the primary model is busy — auto-failover to a slightly cheaper variant to preserve availability.
[01:36] Maya: On failover, do you lose context or the conversation history?
[01:39] Diego: No, we use the same conversation ID and forward the KV cache where compatible. For big architecture differences you'd see a small context window mismatch, but in practice for chat it's seamless most of the time — there can be token offsets, which we call out in the logs.
[01:56] Avery: Let's flip to params: common knobs are temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and the new safety_threshold param for your regulated use case. For triage you probably want deterministic-ish output — so temp 0.0-0.3, top_p 0.8-1.0, and max tokens capped to expected answer length.
[02:15] Maya: If temp is low, does it affect hallucination rates?
[02:18] Diego: Lower temp reduces variance but not guaranteed to remove hallucinations. We recommend prompt engineering + source attribution in the prompt. Also our Optimize tool flags sudden quality regressions when you change model variants.
[02:31] Evan: What about streaming partials while we do function calls or extraction? Any gotchas?
[02:36] Diego: If you're doing function/tool calling we buffer until the call completes and then stream the resulting structured output; streaming partials are better for pure text generation.
[02:44] Avery: On retries — two patterns: client-side idempotency (you attach an idempotency token per user-turn) and server-side automatic retries for transient infra errors. We recommend exponential backoff with jitter and maximum 3 retries for short requests.
[02:58] Tom: What about duplicate messages? If client retries because of a timeout, do we risk double actions?
[03:03] Diego: For stateful actions you must ensure idempotency at the application layer. For generation-only requests we return the same completion when idempotency_key is provided and the request was already processed.
[03:15] Avery: Also note the SDKs expose helpers to manage streaming re-connects and to resume from last token — handy in flaky mobile networks.
[03:26] Maya: Could you show the console observability for a sample test run?
[03:30] Diego: Switching to the metrics tab — here you can see per-route p95 latency, per-token cost breakdown, and token distribution histograms. You can also click into a single request trace and replay the events.
[03:45] Avery: For your cost concerns: Optimize recommends batching, prefix caching, and quantized model variants for background jobs. For triage (interactive) we often suggest small context caching and single-request streaming to keep latency low.
[04:01] Evan: How does prefix caching interact with user-specific data? Our prompts include user ID and a short history.
[04:07] Diego: Prefix caching is best for stable system prompts (instructions). For user-specific dynamic parts we keep them off cache. The console shows cache hit/miss rates per model.
[04:18] Laura: Security question: do you support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM)? We need to ensure keys are not in vendor-managed KMS.
[04:24] Avery: Yes — Redwood Private / Dedicated supports CMEK and integrations with AWS KMS and on-prem HSM. For hosted we offer envelope encryption with KMS integrations and an audit trail; we'll share the integration guide.
[04:38] Laura: And SOC2 and logging retention? We need 7 years for certain audit logs — is that something Redwood can support?
[04:45] Diego: Hosted offers configurable retention windows and exportable audit logs; for very long retention you can ship logs to your S3 via our log export. Dedicated/Private fits stricter retention + air-gapped needs.
[04:58] Maya: Back to reliability — show me an example of a retry scenario and how you'd trace it in the console.
[05:03] Diego: Sure. I'm going to trigger a simulated transient error on the endpoint. (typing) You can see a spike in 503s; the console flagged automatic fallback to the cheaper variant and we have traces that show retry attempts — timestamps and idempotency keys are visible.
[05:23] Tom: Does the fallback change tokenization or model outputs that could break downstream parsers?
[05:28] Diego: It can. That's why we recommend a compatibility matrix — for mission-critical parsing we do A/B test a fallback variant in your shadow traffic before promoting it live.
[05:40] Avery: Quick note about safety: we have a streaming safety filter that can short-circuit responses flagged with high safety_threshold scores. For healthcare triage you might want stricter thresholds which we can tune.
[05:55] Maya: How would we measure quality regressions over time?
[05:58] Diego: Use Redwood Optimize connected to your eval set — you can run periodic evals on your fixed prompt set (we call them canaries) and get alerts on metric regressions, e.g., answer accuracy, hallucination rate, and latency increase.
[06:14] Evan: Could you run a small live test with two sample triage prompts? One short, one long.
[06:19] Diego: Yep. Running short prompt now. (typing) Streaming chunk 1... chunk 2... [quiet typing sounds] The short prompt completes in about 120ms for network + model time in this sandbox.
[06:35] Maya: That's promising. What about cost per request?
[06:38] Avery: Cost depends on tokens. For short triage snippets you're mostly paying for the response tokens + small request tokens. We'll produce a sample cost calc in the pricing sheet for expected token lengths.
[06:49] Diego: Now running the longer prompt — we're showing partials and you can see intermittent re-connect handling. I artificially limited max_tokens to 150 so the response truncates, which is safer for bounded UIs.
[07:05] Tom: If we need completions guaranteed to finish, do you support streaming until EOS across retries?
[07:10] Diego: Yes, but you should set a higher timeout and use streaming resume — the SDK has a resume token if a connection drops mid-stream.
[07:21] Maya: Any gotchas for mobile clients?
[07:24] Diego: Network churn — use small streaming chunks and client-side stitching; also consider putting a local fallback and do server-side reranks to avoid heavy compute on the device.
[07:36] Avery: Let's touch briefly on quotas and rate limits. Hosted has per-project quotas and per-route rate limits; for bursty traffic we recommend Dedicated or reserved burst capacity if you need guaranteed throughput.
[07:51] Evan: For SLA, what are the uptime guarantees for hosted?
[07:54] Avery: Hosted comes with best-effort availability but we provide SLOs for dedicated tiers. For enterprise-grade SLAs you can look at Dedicated where we commit latency / uptime and offer on-call support.
[08:06] Maya: On compliance, if we go hosted and need HIPAA, is there a path?
[08:11] Diego: Hosted can support HIPAA with a Business Associate Agreement and certain data routing restrictions; we typically recommend Dedicated or Private for very sensitive PHI.
[08:23] Maya: Ok. Could you show us how to set a per-route safety threshold in the console?
[08:27] Diego: Sure, settings -> routes -> choose chat-triage route, safety_threshold slider here; you can apply a policy that blocks or redacts content when the threshold is exceeded.
[08:40] Tom: How do we test the threshold without impacting production?
[08:43] Avery: Use canary routing: send a fraction of traffic to the new policy or run shadow traffic. The console will show a side-by-side comparison.
[08:54] Evan: We're interested in measuring tokens-per-request distribution. Can you export histograms?
[08:58] Diego: Yes — export CSV from the token histogram pane, or hook to the API to stream metrics.
[09:06] Maya: This is great. One more question on retries: we worry about duplicate downstream side-effects in our ticketing system if the LLM suggests 'create ticket' and we auto-execute. How do we avoid that?
[09:18] Diego: Two-pronged approach: 1) idempotency on action execution (transactional checks), 2) use the LLM only for suggestions and require explicit confirmation before executing side-effects. We also log predictions with ids to reconcile if duplicates appear.
[09:35] Avery: Wrapping up — my commitments are the pricing sheet, decision matrix, and security docs; Diego will provision the sandbox and run the triage benchmark. We'll aim to get the POC kickoff on the week of 2027-05-24.
[09:52] Maya: Sounds good. Quick ask: can you run the benchmark against both hosted and dedicated (simulated) so we can see delta in latency and cost?
[09:59] Diego: Yep, we'll do hosted baseline and a simulated dedicated profile with lower p95 latency but different cost assumptions.
[10:09] Laura: I'll send over the compliance questionnaire later today.
[10:12] Evan: Thanks everyone.
[10:14] Avery: Thanks — we'll follow up with links.
[10:18] [meeting ends]

Notes: occasional transcript noise, speaker overlaps and auto-caption errors present. Links mentioned in chat: pricing sheet (internal link), security docs: https://redwood.example.com/security/brightwave, sandbox invite: https://console.redwood.example.com/sandbox/invite/CRM-BW-2027-1192
